## 6. Algorithms and computational content

The results of Sections 3 and 4 are effective, and each admits a direct algorithmic test. We describe three.

### 6.1 Frobenius congruence verification in $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_{n}]$

Represent elements of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_{n}]$ as integer polynomials modulo the $n$-th cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_{n}(X)$; $\zeta$ is the class of $X$. The power map $\sigma_{m}$ acts by $f(X) \mapsto f(X^{m}) \bmod \Phi_{n}$. To test Theorem A for a prime $p$ and a random $x$: compute $\sigma_{p}(x) - x^{p}$ in $\mathbb{Z}[X]/\Phi_{n}$ and check that all coefficients are divisible by $p$. Complexity: $O(\log p)$ polynomial multiplications of degree $< \varphi(n)$ with coefficients of bounded size, i.e. $\widetilde{O}(\varphi(n)^{2}\log p)$ bit operations by schoolbook arithmetic.

### 6.2 Frobenius search and rigidity check at a prime

Given $n$, a prime $p \nmid n$, and a prime $Q$ of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_{n}]$ above $p$ (concretely: reduce mod $p$ and pick an irreducible factor $g$ of $\Phi_{n}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$, so $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]/Q \simeq \mathbb{F}_{p}[X]/g$), enumerate all $\varphi(n)$ candidate endomorphisms $\sigma_{m}$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$, and test the Frobenius condition on a generating set. Theorem C predicts exactly one survivor, namely $m \equiv p \pmod n$. This is a direct empirical test of both existence and rigidity, and is the cleanest computational signature of the theory: the search space has size $\varphi(n)$ and the answer is always a single point.

### 6.3 Class-number-driven Hilbert class field degree prediction

For an imaginary quadratic field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$, the class number $h_{K}$ can be computed by counting reduced binary quadratic forms of discriminant $D$: triples $(a,b,c)$ with $b^{2}-4ac = D$, $|b| \le a \le c$, and $b \ge 0$ when $|b| = a$ or $a = c$. Theorem E(1) then predicts the degree of any Hilbert class field of $K$; Theorem E(3) predicts triviality exactly for the nine Heegner discriminants with $h = 1$. Complexity: $O(|D|)$ form enumeration with the bound $a \le \sqrt{|D|/3}$.

---

## 7. Applications and interpretation

**7.1 Reciprocity as congruence.** Theorem A localises the content of cyclotomic reciprocity in two classical congruences (Fermat, and $p \mid \binom{p}{k}$). This has practical value: verifying that a proposed automorphism is a Frobenius requires no computation of ramification indices, decomposition groups, or inertia, only a divisibility check on the generator.

**7.2 Non-maximal orders and ramified primes.** Because Theorems A–C never require $S$ to be integrally closed, they apply verbatim to non-maximal orders $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta] \subseteq \mathcal{O}_{L}$ (and, over other bases, to orders where $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta] \neq \mathcal{O}_{L}$). Because they never require $Q$ to be unramified, they also apply at primes dividing the conductor of the order, provided only $n \notin Q$. This is genuinely wider than the classical statement.

**7.3 A design principle for the existence problem.** Theorem E says the *shape* of a Hilbert class field is determined before construction: degree $h_{K}$, abelian, trivial iff $h_{K} = 1$. Any constructive attempt can therefore be checked cheaply against three invariants. In particular constructions producing a nonabelian group, or a degree different from $h_{K}$, are wrong independently of any subtlety in the ramification analysis.

**7.4 Explicit generation.** For imaginary quadratic $K$ with small class number, the theory of complex multiplication produces explicit generators of the Hilbert class field as singular moduli $j(\tau)$; Theorem E(1) predicts the degree of the minimal polynomial of such a generator to be exactly $h_{K}$, which is the standard consistency check applied to class polynomials in computational number theory (and the basis of CM-method elliptic curve constructions in cryptography).

---

## 8. Discussion

The picture that emerges is one of pronounced asymmetry.

On the reciprocity side, the cyclotomic case — the case from which the general theory was historically abstracted — is elementary once formulated correctly. The formulation matters: by defining "arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$" as a congruence condition on *all* elements, rather than as a distinguished element of a decomposition group, one obtains a statement provable by induction on the construction of the ring. In this formulation, ramification never enters, and the uniqueness statement becomes *stronger* than the classical one.

On the existence side, everything one can extract from the definition alone is soft. Degree, commutativity, and the triviality criterion are one-line consequences; the substance lies entirely in constructing $H$. The only nontrivial theorem we can prove unconditionally about existence is a nonexistence theorem — that $\mathbb{Q}$ has no everywhere-unramified extension — and it consumes the full strength of geometry of numbers.

This suggests a diagnosis of why the existence theorem is hard: it is not a statement about congruences at all. Congruence conditions cut out *at most one* candidate Frobenius (Theorem C$'$), but they never produce the field in which the candidate lives. Existence requires a genuinely global input — analytic (L-functions), cohomological (Brauer groups), or transcendental (complex multiplication) — that no amount of local congruence analysis will supply.

A secondary observation concerns relativisation. The Hermite–Minkowski route to Theorem G uses the *absolute* discriminant bound $|d_{K}| > 2$, which has no relative analogue: there is no numerical obstruction to a relative extension being everywhere unramified — indeed, for $h_{K} > 1$ such extensions exist and are the point of the whole theory. The relative statement "a base of class number one admits no everywhere-unramified extension" must therefore proceed differently, via triviality of the relative different plus a counting argument, and is a genuine theorem rather than a bound.

---

## 9. Future directions

**Frobenius rigidity beyond cyclotomic rings.** Let $S$ be a domain generated over $\mathbb{Z}$ by a single element $\theta$, and let $Q$ be a prime of $S$ with residue field of prime cardinality $p$. Is an arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$ unique whenever it exists, without any unramifiedness hypothesis? We prove this for $\theta$ a root of unity of order invertible modulo $Q$. It is falsifiable by exhibiting a monogenic $S = \mathbb{Z}[\theta]$, a prime $Q$, and two distinct endomorphisms both congruent to $x \mapsto x^{p}$ modulo $Q$. Since uniqueness is classical under unramifiedness, any counterexample must be ramified at $Q$; the natural candidate is $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-3}]$ at $Q = (2, 1+\sqrt{-3})$.

**Everywhere-unramified rigidity over a base of class number one.** If $K$ is a number field with $h_{K} = 1$, is every finite extension $H/K$ unramified at every finite prime *and* every infinite place necessarily equal to $K$? We prove the case $K = \mathbb{Q}$ via the different and Hermite–Minkowski. Falsifying it would require a field of trivial class group carrying a nontrivial everywhere-unramified extension. The step that does not generalise is the discriminant bound; the relative proof must go through triviality of the relative different $\mathfrak{d}_{H/K} = (1)$.

**Degree obstruction as a falsifiability criterion.** Every Hilbert class field datum over $K$ has degree exactly $h_{K}$, so a candidate extension of the wrong degree is immediately excluded. Systematising this as a search procedure over candidate extensions of bounded discriminant would make the existence problem for fixed small $K$ genuinely computational.

**Idèlic realisation of the unramified correspondence.** Construct the canonical surjection from the idèle class group of $K$ onto $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal{O}_{K})$, identify its kernel with the subgroup generated by archimedean components and local unit groups, and prove that pullback identifies ideal-class characters exactly with idèle-class characters trivial on that kernel. This would place Theorem D inside its natural framework and give an intrinsic definition of the Artin map, independent of a chosen generator.

**Principal ideal theorem.** For a Hilbert class field $H/K$, prove that extension of ideals sends every nonzero fractional ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ to a principal fractional ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{H}$; equivalently, that the induced homomorphism $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal{O}_{K}) \to \mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal{O}_{H})$ is zero. This is a genuinely group-theoretic statement (Artin's reduction to the transfer map), and is the natural next milestone once existence is available.

**Explicit imaginary-quadratic generators.** For every imaginary quadratic field of class number at most $4$, construct a singular modulus generating its Hilbert class field, and prove that its minimal polynomial has degree equal to the class number and splitting field unramified over the quadratic base.

---

## 10. Conclusion

We have proved that the cyclotomic case of Artin reciprocity is a theorem about congruences in monogenic rings: a ring endomorphism sending a generator $\zeta$ to $\zeta^{p}$ is congruent to the $p$-th power map modulo $p$ on the entire ring, and conversely an arithmetic Frobenius at a prime $Q$ with residue cardinality $p$ sends a root of unity of order invertible modulo $Q$ exactly to its $p$-th power. Together these give an if-and-only-if characterisation and an unconditional uniqueness statement that dispenses with the classical unramifiedness hypothesis, and they identify the classical Artin map $[p] \mapsto (\zeta \mapsto \zeta^{p})$ on cyclotomic fields with the arithmetic Frobenius on the order $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]$.

Separately, we have shown that a Hilbert class field datum for a number field $K$ — a finite Galois extension unramified at every finite prime together with an isomorphism of its Galois group onto the ideal class group — is forced to have degree $h_{K}$ and abelian Galois group, is trivial exactly when $h_{K} = 1$, is realised trivially when $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ is principal, and over $\mathbb{Q}$ is necessarily trivial by the different-ideal and Minkowski discriminant argument. The existence problem thus stands isolated: all its soft consequences are settled, and what remains is exactly the hard, global construction.

all $x$ in the subring $\ZZ[\zeta]$ generated by $\zeta$. Conversely, if $S$ is a
domain, $\zeta \in S$ satisfies $\zeta^{n} = 1$, $Q \subset S$ is a prime with
residue cardinality $p$ over a base ring $R$, and $n \notin Q$, then any
arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$ sends $\zeta$ to $\zeta^{p}$ exactly. Consequently,
for $S = \ZZ[\zeta]$ monogenic over $\ZZ$ with $p \in Q$ and $n \notin Q$, an
$R$-algebra endomorphism is an arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$ if and only if it is
the power map $\zeta \mapsto \zeta^{p}$; and the arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$ is
unique \emph{with no unramifiedness hypothesis}. Specialising to the cyclotomic
field $\QQ(\zeta_{n})$, the canonical isomorphism $(\ZZ/n)^{\times} \simeq
\Gal(\QQ(\zeta_{n})/\QQ)$ evaluated at the class of a prime $p \nmid n$ restricts
on the order $\ZZ[\zeta]$ to the arithmetic Frobenius at every prime of
$\ZZ[\zeta]$ above $p$, and is the only such endomorphism.

We then isolate the existence assertion for Hilbert class fields as a bundled
datum---a finite Galois extension $H/K$, unramified at all finite primes, with an
isomorphism $\Gal(H/K) \simeq \Cl(\OO_{K})$---and derive its unconditional
consequences: the degree equals the class number; the Galois group is abelian;
the datum is trivial exactly when $h_{K}=1$; any two data over the same base have
equal degree; and the datum exists with $H = K$ whenever $\OO_{K}$ is a principal
ideal ring. As a consistency test we prove, via the different ideal and the
Minkowski discriminant bound, that a number field unramified at every finite
prime over $\ZZ$ equals $\QQ$, whence every Hilbert class field datum over $\QQ$
is trivial.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The two halves of class field theory}

Class field theory asserts a dictionary between the arithmetic of a number field
$K$ and the abelian extensions of $K$. Its two halves are of very different
characters.

\emph{Reciprocity}: given an abelian extension $H/K$ unramified at a prime
$\mathfrak{p}$, there is a canonical Artin symbol
$\left(\frac{H/K}{\mathfrak{p}}\right) \in \Gal(H/K)$ characterised by a
congruence, and $\mathfrak{p} \mapsto \left(\frac{H/K}{\mathfrak{p}}\right)$
extends to a surjection from a ray class group.

\emph{Existence}: every open subgroup of finite index in a suitable id\`ele class
group is a norm group. The distinguished case is the \emph{Hilbert class field}:
a finite extension $H/K$, unramified everywhere, with $\Gal(H/K) \simeq
\Cl(\OO_{K})$.

The archetype for reciprocity is the cyclotomic case over $\QQ$: the Galois group
of $\QQ(\zeta_{n})/\QQ$ is $(\ZZ/n)^{\times}$ via $m \mapsto (\zeta \mapsto
\zeta^{m})$, and the Artin symbol at a prime $p \nmid n$ is the class of $p$.
This paper asks what that archetype actually costs, and---separately---what one
can say about a Hilbert class field before constructing it.

\subsection{Results}

Section~\ref{sec:frob} shows the cyclotomic archetype is a theorem about
congruences in commutative rings, requiring neither Galois theory nor
ramification theory, and valid for non-maximal orders and ramified primes. The
main statements are Theorems~\ref{thm:A}, \ref{thm:B}, \ref{thm:C} and
\ref{thm:Cprime}; Section~\ref{sec:cyc} deduces the classical cyclotomic
reciprocity statement (Theorem~\ref{thm:D}). Section~\ref{sec:hcf} analyses the
existence assertion (Theorems~\ref{thm:E}, \ref{thm:F} and \ref{thm:G}).

Two points deserve emphasis. First, \emph{uniqueness of the Frobenius without
unramifiedness}: standard formulations obtain uniqueness from the isomorphism of
the decomposition group with the residue Galois group, which requires
unramifiedness. Theorem~\ref{thm:Cprime} bypasses this, because a ring
homomorphism is determined by the image of a generator and that image is forced.
Second, \emph{falsifiability of the existence programme}: Theorem~\ref{thm:E}
converts existence into a search with a known target degree and group structure,
and Theorem~\ref{thm:G} supplies the first nontrivial consistency test.

\section{Notation and definitions}

All rings are commutative with $1$; all homomorphisms are unital.

\begin{definition}[Adjoined subring]
For a commutative ring $A$ and $\zeta \in A$, write $\ZZ[\zeta] \subseteq A$ for
the smallest subring containing $\zeta$, i.e.\ the image of the evaluation map
$\ZZ[X] \to A$, $X \mapsto \zeta$. It satisfies the induction principle: any
subset containing the image of $\ZZ$ and $\zeta$, and closed under addition and
multiplication, contains $\ZZ[\zeta]$. We say $A$ is \emph{monogenic over $\ZZ$
with generator $\zeta$} if $\ZZ[\zeta] = A$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Residue cardinality and arithmetic Frobenius]
Let $R \to S$ be a ring map and $Q \subseteq S$ an ideal, with contraction
$Q \cap R$. Put $f(Q) := \#\bigl(R/(Q \cap R)\bigr)$. An $R$-algebra endomorphism
$\sigma : S \to S$ is an \emph{arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$} if
\[
  \sigma(x) - x^{f(Q)} \in Q \qquad \text{for all } x \in S .
\]
\end{definition}

For a number field $K$ we write $\OO_{K}$, $\Cl(\OO_{K})$, $h_{K} =
\#\Cl(\OO_{K})$, $d_{K}$, and $\dif_{K/\QQ}$ for the ring of integers, class
group, class number, discriminant and different ideal. A prime $P$ of $\OO_{K}$
is \emph{unramified over $\ZZ$} if the localisation $(\OO_{K})_{P}$ is formally
unramified over $\ZZ$. An element $\zeta$ of a field $L$ is a \emph{primitive
$n$-th root of unity} if it has exact order $n$ in $L^{\times}$; then
$L = \QQ(\zeta)$ is the $n$-th cyclotomic field, of degree $\varphi(n)$ over
$\QQ$, and $\ZZ[\zeta] \subseteq L$ is the order generated by $\zeta$.

\section{Frobenius in monogenic rings}\label{sec:frob}

\subsection{The congruence}

\begin{theorem}[Frobenius congruence]\label{thm:A}
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $p$ a prime number, $\zeta \in A$, and
$\sigma : A \to A$ a ring homomorphism with $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{p}$. Then for
every $x \in \ZZ[\zeta] \subseteq A$,
\[
  \sigma(x) - x^{p} \in pA .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $J := pA$ and $T := \{x \in A : \sigma(x) - x^{p} \in J\}$. We show $T$
contains the image of $\ZZ$ and $\zeta$, and is closed under sums and products;
the induction principle then gives $\ZZ[\zeta] \subseteq T$.

\emph{(i) Integers.} For $m \in \ZZ$ with image $\bar m \in A$, Fermat's little
theorem gives $m^{p} - m = pk$ in $\ZZ$, hence $\bar m^{p} - \bar m = p\bar k \in
J$. Since $\sigma(\bar m) = \bar m$, we get $\sigma(\bar m) - \bar m^{p} \in J$.

\emph{(ii) Generator.} $\sigma(\zeta) - \zeta^{p} = 0 \in J$.

\emph{(iii) Products.} If $\sigma(x) = x^{p} + pu$ and $\sigma(y) = y^{p} + pv$,
then
\[
 \sigma(xy) - (xy)^{p} = (\sigma(x) - x^{p})\sigma(y) + x^{p}(\sigma(y) - y^{p})
 = p\bigl(u\,\sigma(y) + x^{p}v\bigr) \in J .
\]

\emph{(iv) Sums.} Since $p \mid \binom{p}{k}$ for $0 < k < p$,
\[
 (x+y)^{p} = x^{p} + y^{p} + p\,w, \qquad
 w := \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \tfrac{1}{p}\tbinom{p}{k}\,x^{p-k}y^{k} \in A ,
\]
each $\frac{1}{p}\binom{p}{k}$ being an integer. Hence
$\sigma(x+y) - (x+y)^{p} = p(u+v-w) \in J$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
No hypotheses on $A$ beyond commutativity are needed: $A$ need not be a domain,
$\zeta$ need not be a root of unity, and no prime ideal appears. Step (iv) is the
only use of primality, and is the mechanism making $x \mapsto x^{p}$ additive in
characteristic $p$.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Monogenic form]\label{cor:mono}
If in addition $\ZZ[\zeta] = A$, then $\sigma(x) \equiv x^{p} \pmod{pA}$ for all
$x \in A$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Rigidity of endomorphisms}

\begin{lemma}[Generator extensionality]\label{lem:ext}
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with $\ZZ[\zeta] = A$. If $\sigma, \tau : A \to A$
are ring homomorphisms with $\sigma(\zeta) = \tau(\zeta)$, then $\sigma = \tau$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The equaliser $\{x : \sigma(x) = \tau(x)\}$ contains the image of $\ZZ$ and
$\zeta$, and is closed under sums and products; by induction it contains
$\ZZ[\zeta] = A$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Power maps are Frobenius maps}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:power}
Let $R \to S$ be a ring map, $\zeta \in S$ with $\ZZ[\zeta] = S$, $p$ a prime,
and $Q \subseteq S$ an ideal with $f(Q) = p$ and $p \in Q$. Then every
$R$-algebra endomorphism $\sigma$ of $S$ with $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{p}$ is an
arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $x \in S$, Corollary~\ref{cor:mono} gives $\sigma(x) - x^{p} = py$ for some
$y \in S$; since $p \in Q$, $py \in Q$. As $f(Q) = p$, this is exactly the
Frobenius condition.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Frobenius maps are power maps}

\begin{theorem}[Frobenius determines the generator]\label{thm:B}
Let $R \to S$ be a ring map with $S$ an integral domain. Let $\zeta \in S$ satisfy
$\zeta^{n} = 1$ for some $n \geq 1$, and let $Q \subseteq S$ be an ideal with
$n \cdot 1_{S} \notin Q$ and $f(Q) = p$. If $\sigma$ is an arithmetic Frobenius at
$Q$, then $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{p}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $a := \sigma(\zeta)$, $b := \zeta^{p}$.

\emph{Step 1.} $a^{n} = \sigma(\zeta^{n}) = \sigma(1) = 1$ and
$b^{n} = (\zeta^{n})^{p} = 1$.

\emph{Step 2.} Applying the Frobenius property to $x = \zeta$ gives
$a - b \in Q$.

\emph{Step 3.} By Step 1,
\[
 0 = a^{n} - b^{n} = (a-b)\,\Sigma, \qquad
 \Sigma := \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a^{i}b^{\,n-1-i}.
\]
Assume $a \neq b$; as $S$ is a domain and $a-b \neq 0$, we get $\Sigma = 0$.

\emph{Step 4.} By Step 2, $a \equiv b \pmod Q$, so $a^{i}b^{\,n-1-i} \equiv
b^{\,n-1} \pmod Q$ for each $i$, whence $\Sigma \equiv n\,b^{\,n-1} \pmod Q$ and
therefore $n\,b^{\,n-1} \in Q$.

\emph{Step 5.} From $b\cdot b^{\,n-1} = 1$, $b^{\,n-1}$ is a unit; multiplying by
its inverse gives $n \cdot 1_{S} \in Q$, a contradiction. Hence $a = b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The hypothesis $n \notin Q$ says precisely that $X^{n}-1$ stays separable modulo
$Q$; separability is what prevents distinct roots of unity from colliding, and
Steps 3--5 upgrade the congruence $a \equiv b$ to the equality $a = b$. The
hypothesis cannot be dropped: in $\ZZ[i]$ with $n = 4$ and $Q = (1+i)$ one has
$4 \in Q$, and both complex conjugation and the identity are congruent to the
squaring map modulo $Q$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Characterisation and rigidity}

\begin{theorem}[Characterisation]\label{thm:C}
Let $R \to S$ be a ring map with $S$ a domain, $\zeta \in S$ with $\zeta^{n} = 1$
and $\ZZ[\zeta] = S$. Let $Q \subseteq S$ be an ideal with $n \notin Q$,
$f(Q) = p$ a prime, and $p \in Q$. Then for an $R$-algebra endomorphism $\sigma$
of $S$,
\[
 \sigma \text{ is an arithmetic Frobenius at } Q \iff \sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{p}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorems~\ref{thm:B} and \ref{thm:power}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rigidity, no unramifiedness]\label{thm:Cprime}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:C} (with $p \in Q$ not required), if
$\sigma$ and $\tau$ are arithmetic Frobenius maps at $Q$, then $\sigma = \tau$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:B} gives $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{p} = \tau(\zeta)$; apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:ext}.
\end{proof}

Classical uniqueness of the Frobenius element assumes $Q$ unramified.
Theorem~\ref{thm:Cprime} replaces that hypothesis by monogenicity, obtaining
uniqueness even at ramified primes, provided the order of the generating root of
unity is invertible modulo $Q$.

\section{Cyclotomic reciprocity over $\QQ$}\label{sec:cyc}

Fix $n \geq 1$ and let $L = \QQ(\zeta)$ with $\zeta$ a primitive $n$-th root of
unity, so $[L:\QQ] = \varphi(n)$.

\begin{definition}[Artin map]
The \emph{cyclotomic Artin map} is the isomorphism
$\Art : (\ZZ/n\ZZ)^{\times} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \Gal(L/\QQ)$ inverse to the
injection sending $\sigma$ to the unique class $u$ with $\sigma(\eta) = \eta^{u}$
for every primitive $n$-th root $\eta$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Independence of the chosen primitive root]
Let $\zeta, \zeta'$ be primitive $n$-th roots of unity in $L$ and
$\sigma \in \Gal(L/\QQ)$. The exponent classes determined by $\zeta$ and $\zeta'$
coincide.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $\zeta' = \zeta^{k}$ with $\gcd(k,n) = 1$. Then
$\zeta^{uk} = \sigma(\zeta)^{k} = \sigma(\zeta') = (\zeta')^{u'} =
\zeta^{ku'}$, and since $\zeta$ has exact order $n$, $uk \equiv ku' \pmod n$;
invertibility of $k$ gives $u \equiv u'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Catalog description]\label{lem:catalog}
For $m$ coprime to $n$ and $\sigma \in \Gal(L/\QQ)$, the exponent class of
$\sigma$ is $[m]$ if and only if $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{m}$. Hence $\Art([m])$
is the power map $\sigma_{m} : \zeta \mapsto \zeta^{m}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If the class is $[m]$ then $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{m \bmod n} = \zeta^{m}$ using
$\zeta^{n}=1$. Conversely, comparing $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{m}$ with
$\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{u}$ and using that $\zeta$ has exact order $n$ gives
$u \equiv m \pmod n$.
\end{proof}

Let $\OO := \ZZ[\zeta] \subseteq L$.

\begin{lemma}[Self-generation]\label{lem:self}
As a ring in its own right, $\OO$ is generated over $\ZZ$ by $\zeta$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The inclusion $\OO \hookrightarrow L$ is an injective ring map sending
$\zeta \mapsto \zeta$, hence carries the subring generated by $\zeta$ inside
$\OO$ onto $\ZZ[\zeta] = \OO$; injectivity forces equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Stability]\label{lem:stab}
If $\sigma : L \to L$ is a ring homomorphism with $\sigma(\zeta) \in \OO$, then
$\sigma(\OO) \subseteq \OO$ and $\sigma$ restricts to a $\ZZ$-algebra
endomorphism of $\OO$. In particular $\sigma_{m}$ restricts to $\OO$ for every
$m$ coprime to $n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\sigma^{-1}(\OO) \cap \OO$ is a subring of $L$ containing $\ZZ$ and $\zeta$,
hence contains $\ZZ[\zeta] = \OO$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cyclotomic reciprocity over $\QQ$]\label{thm:D}
Let $\zeta$ be a primitive $n$-th root of unity in $L$, $\OO = \ZZ[\zeta]$, and
$p$ a prime with $\gcd(p,n) = 1$. Let $Q \subseteq \OO$ be an ideal with
$\#(\ZZ/(Q\cap\ZZ)) = p$ and $p \in Q$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\Art([p])$ preserves $\OO$ and its restriction is an arithmetic Frobenius
at $Q$;
\item if moreover $n \notin Q$, every $\ZZ$-algebra endomorphism of $\OO$ that is
an arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$ equals $\Art([p])|_{\OO}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) By Lemma~\ref{lem:catalog}, $\Art([p])(\zeta) = \zeta^{p} \in \OO$, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:stab} it restricts to an endomorphism $\sigma$ of $\OO$ with
$\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^{p}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:self}, $\OO$ is monogenic with
generator $\zeta$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:power} applies with $R = \ZZ$.

(2) $\OO$ is a domain and $\zeta^{n} = 1$; Theorem~\ref{thm:B} forces
$\varphi(\zeta) = \zeta^{p}$ for any Frobenius $\varphi$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:ext} concludes.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
For primes $p \nmid n$, the arithmetic Frobenius on $\ZZ[\zeta]$ at a prime $Q$
above $p$ is independent of the choice of $Q$ and equals $\Art([p])|_{\OO}$.
\end{corollary}

The only arithmetic inputs are Fermat's little theorem, divisibility of interior
binomial coefficients by $p$, and separability of $X^{n}-1$ modulo $Q$.

\section{Hilbert class field data}\label{sec:hcf}

\begin{definition}[Hilbert class field datum]
Let $K \subseteq H$ be number fields. A \emph{Hilbert class field datum} for
$(K,H)$ consists of: finiteness of $H$ as a $K$-vector space; the extension
$H/K$ being Galois; unramifiedness of every prime of $\OO_{H}$ over $\OO_{K}$;
and an isomorphism $\Art : \Gal(H/K) \xrightarrow{\sim} \Cl(\OO_{K})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Structural constraints]\label{thm:E}
Let $(H/K,\Art)$ be a Hilbert class field datum. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $[H:K] = h_{K}$;
\item $\Gal(H/K)$ is abelian, so $H/K$ is abelian;
\item the structure map $K \to H$ is bijective if and only if $h_{K} = 1$;
\item any two Hilbert class field data over the same $K$ have equal degree.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) For a finite Galois extension $\#\Gal(H/K) = [H:K]$, and $\Art$ gives
$\#\Gal(H/K) = \#\Cl(\OO_{K}) = h_{K}$.

(2) $\Art(\sigma\tau) = \Art(\sigma)\Art(\tau) = \Art(\tau)\Art(\sigma) =
\Art(\tau\sigma)$ since $\Cl(\OO_{K})$ is abelian; injectivity of $\Art$ gives
$\sigma\tau = \tau\sigma$.

(3) The structure map is injective. It is surjective iff $[H:K] = 1$: surjectivity
gives a $K$-linear isomorphism $K \simeq H$; conversely if $[H:K] = 1$ the image
is a one-dimensional subspace of a one-dimensional space. Now apply (1).

(4) Both degrees equal $h_{K}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Realisation in the principal case]\label{thm:F}
If $\OO_{K}$ is a principal ideal ring, then $H := K$ carries a Hilbert class
field datum for $K$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$K/K$ is finite Galois of degree $1$; localisations of $\OO_{K}$ at its primes
are formally unramified over $\OO_{K}$; and both $\Gal(K/K)$ and $\Cl(\OO_{K})$
are trivial, so a (unique) isomorphism exists.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Trivial different]\label{thm:diff}
If every prime of $\OO_{K}$ is unramified over $\ZZ$, then $\dif_{K/\QQ} = (1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Otherwise $\dif_{K/\QQ}$ lies in a maximal ideal $P$, so $P \mid \dif_{K/\QQ}$;
but a prime divides the different exactly when it ramifies, contradicting the
hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:disc}
Under the same hypothesis, $|d_{K}| = 1$, since $|d_{K}|$ is the absolute norm of
$\dif_{K/\QQ}$ and the unit ideal has norm $1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Hermite--Minkowski]\label{thm:G}
If every prime of $\OO_{K}$ is unramified over $\ZZ$, then $[K:\QQ] = 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $n := [K:\QQ] > 1$. Minkowski's bound, obtained by applying the convex
body theorem to $\OO_{K}$ embedded as a full lattice in
$\RR^{r_{1}} \times \CC^{r_{2}}$ of covolume proportional to $\sqrt{|d_{K}|}$,
gives $|d_{K}| \geq (\pi/4)^{2r_{2}} n^{2n}/(n!)^{2} > 2$ for $n \geq 2$. This
contradicts Corollary~\ref{cor:disc}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Falsifiability test over $\QQ$, passed]
Every Hilbert class field datum over $\QQ$ is trivial: if $(H/\QQ,\Art)$ is such a
datum then $[H:\QQ] = 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Unramifiedness over $\OO_{\QQ}$ implies unramifiedness over $\ZZ$, since
$\ZZ \to \OO_{\QQ}$ is surjective, hence formally unramified, and formal
unramifiedness composes. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:G}.
\end{proof}

This agrees with Theorem~\ref{thm:E}(3) together with $h_{\QQ} = 1$; the two
derivations are independent, so their agreement is a genuine consistency check.

\section{Computational content}

The results are effective. Represent elements of $\ZZ[\zeta_{n}]$ as integer
polynomials modulo the $n$-th cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_{n}(X)$, with $\zeta$
the class of $X$; then $\sigma_{m}$ acts by $f(X) \mapsto f(X^{m}) \bmod
\Phi_{n}$. Testing Theorem~\ref{thm:A} amounts to checking that all coefficients
of $\sigma_{p}(x) - x^{p}$ are divisible by $p$, costing
$\widetilde{O}(\varphi(n)^{2}\log p)$ bit operations.

Testing Theorems~\ref{thm:C} and \ref{thm:Cprime} is equally direct: fix $p \nmid
n$, take a prime $Q$ above $p$ by choosing an irreducible factor $g$ of $\Phi_{n}$
over $\FF_{p}$, so $\ZZ[\zeta]/Q \simeq \FF_{p}[X]/g$, and enumerate the
$\varphi(n)$ candidate endomorphisms $\sigma_{m}$. Exactly one satisfies the
Frobenius condition, namely $m \equiv p \pmod n$.

For imaginary quadratic $K = \QQ(\sqrt{-d})$ of discriminant $D$, the class number
is the number of reduced binary quadratic forms $(a,b,c)$ with $b^{2}-4ac = D$,
$|b| \le a \le c$, and $b \ge 0$ when $|b| = a$ or $a = c$; by
Theorem~\ref{thm:E}(1) this is the degree of any Hilbert class field of $K$.

\section{Discussion}

The picture is one of pronounced asymmetry. On the reciprocity side, the
cyclotomic case is elementary once formulated correctly: defining ``arithmetic
Frobenius at $Q$'' as a congruence condition on all elements, rather than as a
distinguished element of a decomposition group, yields a statement provable by
induction on the construction of the ring, in which ramification never enters and
the uniqueness statement becomes stronger than the classical one.

On the existence side, everything extractable from the definition alone is soft:
degree, commutativity and the triviality criterion are one-line consequences,
while the substance lies entirely in constructing $H$. The only nontrivial
unconditional theorem about existence available here is a nonexistence
theorem---$\QQ$ has no everywhere-unramified extension---and it consumes the full
strength of geometry of numbers. This suggests a diagnosis: congruence conditions
cut out at most one candidate Frobenius but never produce the field in which it
lives. Existence requires a genuinely global input.

A secondary observation concerns relativisation. The route to Theorem~\ref{thm:G}
uses the absolute discriminant bound, which has no relative analogue---indeed for
$h_{K} > 1$ everywhere-unramified relative extensions exist and are the point of
the theory. The relative statement must proceed via triviality of the relative
different.

\section{Future directions}

\emph{Frobenius rigidity beyond cyclotomic rings.} Let $S$ be a domain generated
over $\ZZ$ by a single $\theta$ and $Q$ a prime with residue field of prime
cardinality $p$. Is an arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$ unique whenever it exists,
without unramifiedness? Proved here for $\theta$ a root of unity of order
invertible modulo $Q$. A counterexample must be ramified at $Q$; the natural
candidate is $\ZZ[\sqrt{-3}]$ at $Q = (2, 1+\sqrt{-3})$.

\emph{Everywhere-unramified rigidity over a base of class number one.} If
$h_{K} = 1$, is every extension $H/K$ unramified at all finite primes and all
infinite places equal to $K$? Proved here for $K = \QQ$; the relative proof must
go through $\dif_{H/K} = (1)$.

\emph{Degree obstruction as a search criterion.} Since any Hilbert class field
datum has degree $h_{K}$, candidate extensions of the wrong degree are excluded
immediately; systematising this over extensions of bounded discriminant makes the
existence problem for fixed small $K$ computational.

\emph{Id\`elic realisation.} Construct the canonical surjection from the id\`ele
class group of $K$ onto $\Cl(\OO_{K})$, identify its kernel with the subgroup
generated by archimedean components and local unit groups, and prove that
pullback identifies ideal-class characters with id\`ele-class characters trivial
on that kernel.

\emph{Principal ideal theorem.} For a Hilbert class field $H/K$, prove that
extension of ideals sends every nonzero fractional ideal of $\OO_{K}$ to a
principal fractional ideal of $\OO_{H}$; equivalently that
$\Cl(\OO_{K}) \to \Cl(\OO_{H})$ is zero.

\emph{Explicit imaginary-quadratic generators.} For every imaginary quadratic
field of class number at most $4$, construct a singular modulus generating its
Hilbert class field and prove that its minimal polynomial has degree $h_{K}$ with
splitting field unramified over the quadratic base.

\section{Conclusion}

The cyclotomic case of Artin reciprocity is a theorem about congruences in
monogenic rings: a ring endomorphism sending a generator $\zeta$ to $\zeta^{p}$
is congruent to the $p$-th power map modulo $p$ throughout the ring, and
conversely an arithmetic Frobenius at a prime of residue cardinality $p$ sends a
root of unity of order invertible modulo that prime exactly to its $p$-th power.
Together these give an if-and-only-if characterisation and an unconditional
uniqueness statement dispensing with unramifiedness. Separately, a Hilbert class
field datum is forced to have degree $h_{K}$ and abelian Galois group, is trivial
exactly when $h_{K} = 1$, is realised trivially when $\OO_{K}$ is principal, and
over $\QQ$ is necessarily trivial. The existence problem thus stands isolated:
all its soft consequences are settled, and what remains is the hard global
construction.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Poly = List[int]  # dense coefficient list, index = degree, little-endian


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Polynomial arithmetic over Z and over F_p
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def poly_trim(a: Poly) -> Poly:
    """Remove trailing zero coefficients."""
    b = list(a)
    while b and b[-1] == 0:
        b.pop()
    return b


def poly_add(a: Poly, b: Poly, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
    n = max(len(a), len(b))
    out = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        v = (a[i] if i < len(a) else 0) + (b[i] if i < len(b) else 0)
        out[i] = v % mod if mod else v
    return poly_trim(out)


def poly_sub(a: Poly, b: Poly, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
    n = max(len(a), len(b))
    out = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        v = (a[i] if i < len(a) else 0) - (b[i] if i < len(b) else 0)
        out[i] = v % mod if mod else v
    return poly_trim(out)


def poly_mul(a: Poly, b: Poly, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
    if not a or not b:
        return []
    out = [0] * (len(a) + len(b) - 1)
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai == 0:
            continue
        for j, bj in enumerate(b):
            out[i + j] += ai * bj
    if mod:
        out = [c % mod for c in out]
    return poly_trim(out)


def poly_divmod(a: Poly, b: Poly, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Tuple[Poly, Poly]:
    """Division with remainder; `b` must be monic when working over Z."""
    a = poly_trim(a)
    b = poly_trim(b)
    if not b:
        raise ZeroDivisionError("division by the zero polynomial")
    lead = b[-1]
    if mod:
        inv_lead = pow(lead % mod, -1, mod)
    elif lead not in (1, -1):
        raise ValueError("over Z the divisor must be monic (or -monic)")
    else:
        inv_lead = lead
    q: Poly = [0] * max(0, len(a) - len(b) + 1)
    r = list(a)
    while poly_trim(r) and len(poly_trim(r)) >= len(b):
        r = poly_trim(r)
        shift = len(r) - len(b)
        coeff = (r[-1] * inv_lead) % mod if mod else r[-1] * inv_lead
        q[shift] = coeff % mod if mod else coeff
        for i, bi in enumerate(b):
            r[shift + i] -= coeff * bi
            if mod:
                r[shift + i] %= mod
    return poly_trim(q), poly_trim(r)


def poly_mod(a: Poly, m: Poly, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
    return poly_divmod(a, m, mod)[1]


def poly_gcd_modp(a: Poly, b: Poly, p: int) -> Poly:
    a, b = poly_trim(a), poly_trim(b)
    while b:
        a, b = b, poly_mod(a, b, p)
    if a:
        inv = pow(a[-1], -1, p)
        a = [(c * inv) % p for c in a]
    return a


def poly_str(a: Poly, var: str = "z") -> str:
    a = poly_trim(a)
    if not a:
        return "0"
    parts: List[str] = []
    for i in range(len(a) - 1, -1, -1):
        c = a[i]
        if c == 0:
            continue
        if i == 0:
            parts.append(f"{c:+d}")
        elif i == 1:
            parts.append(f"{c:+d}*{var}")
        else:
            parts.append(f"{c:+d}*{var}^{i}")
    return " ".join(parts)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Cyclotomic polynomials
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def divisors(n: int) -> List[int]:
    return [d for d in range(1, n + 1) if n % d == 0]


def cyclotomic(n: int) -> Poly:
    """Phi_n(X) computed by the recursion X^n - 1 = prod_{d | n} Phi_d(X)."""
    if n == 1:
        return [-1, 1]
    num: Poly = [0] * n + [1]
    num[0] = -1
    for d in divisors(n):
        if d < n:
            num, rem = poly_divmod(num, cyclotomic(d))
            assert not rem, "cyclotomic recursion must divide exactly"
    return num


def euler_phi(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for k in range(1, n + 1) if math.gcd(k, n) == 1)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The ring Z[zeta_n] and its power maps
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class CyclotomicRing:
    """The order Z[zeta_n], represented as Z[X] / Phi_n(X)."""

    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        self.n: int = n
        self.phi: Poly = cyclotomic(n)
        self.degree: int = len(self.phi) - 1

    def reduce(self, a: Poly, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
        return poly_mod(a, self.phi if mod is None else [c % mod for c in self.phi], mod)

    def mul(self, a: Poly, b: Poly, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
        return self.reduce(poly_mul(a, b, mod), mod)

    def power(self, a: Poly, e: int, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
        result: Poly = [1]
        base = self.reduce(a, mod)
        while e:
            if e & 1:
                result = self.mul(result, base, mod)
            base = self.mul(base, base, mod)
            e >>= 1
        return result

    def power_map(self, a: Poly, m: int, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
        """Apply sigma_m : zeta -> zeta^m to the element a(zeta)."""
        out: Poly = []
        for i, c in enumerate(a):
            if c == 0:
                continue
            term = self.power([0, 1], (i * m) % self.n, mod)
            out = poly_add(out, [(c * t) % mod if mod else c * t for t in term], mod)
        return self.reduce(out, mod)

    def random_element(self, bound: int = 5, rng: Optional[random.Random] = None) -> Poly:
        r = rng or random
        return poly_trim([r.randint(-bound, bound) for _ in range(self.degree)])


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 1: the Frobenius congruence sigma(x) = x^p (mod p)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def frobenius_congruence_defect(ring: CyclotomicRing, x: Poly, p: int) -> Poly:
    """Return sigma_p(x) - x^p in Z[zeta_n]; Theorem A says p divides it."""
    return poly_sub(ring.power_map(x, p), ring.power(x, p))


def experiment_frobenius_congruence(trials: int = 4, seed: int = 20260804) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXPERIMENT 1 -- Frobenius congruence:  sigma_p(x) = x^p  (mod p)")
    print("=" * 78)
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    for n, p in [(5, 3), (7, 2), (8, 5), (12, 7)]:
        ring = CyclotomicRing(n)
        print(f"\n  n = {n:2d}   Phi_n = {poly_str(ring.phi)}   deg = {ring.degree}   p = {p}")
        for _ in range(trials):
            x = ring.random_element(4, rng)
            defect = frobenius_congruence_defect(ring, x, p)
            divisible = all(c % p == 0 for c in defect)
            quotient = [c // p for c in defect]
            status = "OK " if divisible else "FAIL"
            print(f"    [{status}] x = {poly_str(x):<28s} "
                  f"(sigma_p(x) - x^p)/p = {poly_str(quotient)}")
            assert divisible, "Theorem A violated"
    print("\n  All defects are divisible by p, as Theorem A predicts.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 2: Frobenius search at a prime Q above p, and uniqueness
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def irreducible_factor_mod_p(ring: CyclotomicRing, p: int) -> Poly:
    """A monic irreducible factor g of Phi_n mod p; Q = (p, g(zeta)) is a prime.

    The residue field Z[zeta]/Q is F_p[X]/(g), of size p^deg(g).  We take a
    factor of degree 1 whenever one exists (i.e. when p = 1 mod n), otherwise we
    split off a factor by trial division by all monic polynomials of small
    degree.  For the small parameters used in the demo this is ample.
    """
    f = [c % p for c in ring.phi]
    d = len(f) - 1
    for deg in range(1, d + 1):
        for coeffs in _monic_polys(deg, p):
            q, r = poly_divmod(f, coeffs, p)
            if not r:
                return coeffs
    raise RuntimeError("no factor found")


def _monic_polys(deg: int, p: int):
    """Enumerate monic polynomials of the given degree over F_p."""
    def rec(prefix: List[int], k: int):
        if k == 0:
            yield prefix + [1]
            return
        for c in range(p):
            yield from rec(prefix + [c], k - 1)
    return rec([], deg)


def is_arith_frobenius(ring: CyclotomicRing, m: int, p: int, g: Poly,
                       test_elements: Sequence[Poly]) -> bool:
    """Test sigma_m(x) = x^p mod Q for Q = (p, g(zeta)), on the given elements."""
    for x in test_elements:
        lhs = poly_mod(ring.power_map(x, m, p), g, p)
        rhs = poly_mod(ring.power(x, p, p), g, p)
        if poly_trim(lhs) != poly_trim(rhs):
            return False
    return True


def experiment_frobenius_search(seed: int = 7) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXPERIMENT 2 -- Frobenius search at Q | p:  exactly one power map wins")
    print("=" * 78)
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    for n, p in [(5, 3), (7, 3), (8, 5), (11, 2), (12, 7)]:
        ring = CyclotomicRing(n)
        g = irreducible_factor_mod_p(ring, p)
        tests = [ring.random_element(3, rng) for _ in range(6)] + [[0, 1], [1, 1]]
        winners = [m for m in range(1, n) if math.gcd(m, n) == 1
                   and is_arith_frobenius(ring, m, p, g, tests)]
        predicted = p % n
        print(f"\n  n = {n:2d}, p = {p}:  residue field F_{p}^{len(g) - 1} "
              f"via g = {poly_str(g, 'X')} mod {p}")
        print(f"    candidates m in (Z/{n})^*  : "
              f"{[m for m in range(1, n) if math.gcd(m, n) == 1]}")
        print(f"    Frobenius maps found       : {winners}")
        print(f"    predicted (m = p mod n)    : [{predicted}]")
        assert winners == [predicted], "Theorem C / rigidity violated"
    print("\n  In every case the Frobenius exists and is unique: it is sigma_p.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 3: sharpness -- a ramified prime where rigidity fails
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def experiment_ramified_failure() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXPERIMENT 3 -- sharpness of the hypothesis  n not in Q")
    print("=" * 78)
    # Z[i] = Z[zeta_4], Phi_4 = X^2 + 1, Q = (1 + i) is the ramified prime over 2.
    # Residue field is F_2, so f(Q) = 2, and 4 = -(1+i)^2 * ... lies in Q.
    ring = CyclotomicRing(4)
    p = 2
    g = [1, 1]  # X + 1 : Phi_4 = X^2 + 1 = (X+1)^2 mod 2
    tests = [[0, 1], [1, 1], [1, 0], [2, 3], [-1, 4], [3, -2]]
    identity_ok = is_arith_frobenius(ring, 1, p, g, tests)
    conj_ok = is_arith_frobenius(ring, 3, p, g, tests)
    print("\n  Ring Z[i] = Z[zeta_4],  Phi_4 = X^2 + 1 = (X+1)^2 mod 2 (RAMIFIED)")
    print("  Prime Q = (2, 1+i), residue field F_2, so f(Q) = 2 and 4 lies in Q.")
    print(f"    identity            (m = 1) is a Frobenius at Q : {identity_ok}")
    print(f"    complex conjugation (m = 3) is a Frobenius at Q : {conj_ok}")
    assert identity_ok and conj_ok
    print("\n  Two DISTINCT Frobenius maps: rigidity fails exactly when the order")
    print("  n of zeta is not invertible mod Q.  The hypothesis is necessary.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 4: class numbers and Hilbert class field degrees
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def class_number_imaginary_quadratic(disc: int) -> int:
    """h(D) for a negative fundamental discriminant D, by counting reduced forms.

    A reduced positive definite form (a, b, c) with b^2 - 4ac = D satisfies
    |b| <= a <= c, and b >= 0 whenever |b| = a or a = c.
    """
    if disc >= 0 or disc % 4 not in (0, 1):
        raise ValueError("D must be a negative discriminant, D = 0 or 1 mod 4")
    count = 0
    a_max = int(math.isqrt(-disc // 3)) + 1
    for a in range(1, a_max + 1):
        for b in range(-a + 1, a + 1):
            num = b * b - disc
            if num % (4 * a):
                continue
            c = num // (4 * a)
            if c < a:
                continue
            if (a == c or abs(b) == a) and b < 0:
                continue
            count += 1
    return count


def fundamental_discriminant(d: int) -> int:
    """Discriminant of Q(sqrt(-d)) for squarefree d > 0."""
    return -d if (-d) % 4 == 1 else -4 * d


def squarefree(m: int) -> bool:
    k = 2
    while k * k <= m:
        if m % (k * k) == 0:
            return False
        k += 1
    return True


def experiment_class_numbers(limit: int = 60) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXPERIMENT 4 -- class numbers h_K and forced Hilbert class field degree")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  K = Q(sqrt(-d));  any Hilbert class field of K has degree exactly h_K,")
    print("  and equals K itself precisely when h_K = 1.\n")
    print(f"    {'d':>4s} {'disc':>6s} {'h_K':>5s}  {'[H:K] forced':>13s}  trivial?")
    trivial: List[int] = []
    by_class_number: Dict[int, List[int]] = {}
    for d in range(1, limit + 1):
        if not squarefree(d):
            continue
        D = fundamental_discriminant(d)
        h = class_number_imaginary_quadratic(D)
        by_class_number.setdefault(h, []).append(d)
        if h == 1:
            trivial.append(d)
        if d <= 30:
            print(f"    {d:4d} {D:6d} {h:5d}  {h:13d}  {'yes' if h == 1 else 'no'}")
    print(f"\n  Class number one for d <= {limit}: {trivial}")
    print("  (These are the Heegner values: 1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163.)")
    for h in sorted(by_class_number)[:6]:
        print(f"    h_K = {h}: d = {by_class_number[h][:10]}")
    assert trivial[:7] == [1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 5: the Minkowski discriminant bound
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def minkowski_discriminant_lower_bound(n: int, r2: int) -> float:
    """(pi/4)^(2 r2) * n^(2n) / (n!)^2 : a lower bound for |d_K| in degree n."""
    return (math.pi / 4.0) ** (2 * r2) * (n ** (2 * n)) / (math.factorial(n) ** 2)


def experiment_minkowski(max_degree: int = 8) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXPERIMENT 5 -- Minkowski bound forces |d_K| > 2 in degree >= 2")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  An everywhere-unramified number field has trivial different, hence")
    print("  |d_K| = 1.  The bound below shows that is impossible unless n = 1.\n")
    print(f"    {'n':>3s}  {'worst-case r2':>13s}  {'min |d_K| bound':>17s}  > 2 ?")
    for n in range(1, max_degree + 1):
        worst = max(range(0, n // 2 + 1),
                    key=lambda r2: -minkowski_discriminant_lower_bound(n, r2))
        bound = minkowski_discriminant_lower_bound(n, worst)
        flag = "yes" if bound > 2 else "no"
        print(f"    {n:3d}  {worst:13d}  {bound:17.4f}  {flag}")
        if n >= 2:
            assert bound > 2, "Minkowski bound unexpectedly weak"
    print("\n  Hence |d_K| = 1 forces [K:Q] = 1: Q has no unramified extension,")
    print("  so every Hilbert class field datum over Q is trivial, matching h_Q = 1.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main() -> None:
    print()
    print("#" * 78)
    print("#  Frobenius rigidity in cyclotomic rings, and Hilbert class field data")
    print("#" * 78)
    experiment_frobenius_congruence()
    experiment_frobenius_search()
    experiment_ramified_failure()
    experiment_class_numbers()
    experiment_minkowski()
    print()
    print("All experiments completed successfully.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    return num


def euler_phi(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for k in range(1, n + 1) if math.gcd(k, n) == 1)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The ring Z[zeta_n] and its power maps
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class CyclotomicRing:
    """The order Z[zeta_n], represented as Z[X] / Phi_n(X)."""

    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        self.n: int = n
        self.phi: Poly = cyclotomic(n)
        self.degree: int = len(self.phi) - 1

    def reduce(self, a: Poly, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
        return poly_mod(a, self.phi if mod is None else [c % mod for c in self.phi], mod)

    def mul(self, a: Poly, b: Poly, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
        return self.reduce(poly_mul(a, b, mod), mod)

    def power(self, a: Poly, e: int, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
        result: Poly = [1]
        base = self.reduce(a, mod)
        while e:
            if e & 1:
                result = self.mul(result, base, mod)
            base = self.mul(base, base, mod)
            e >>= 1
        return result

    def power_map(self, a: Poly, m: int, mod: Optional[int] = None) -> Poly:
        """Apply sigma_m : zeta -> zeta^m to the element a(zeta)."""
        out: Poly = []
        for i, c in enumerate(a):
            if c == 0:
                continue
            term = self.power([0, 1], (i * m) % self.n, mod)
            out = poly_add(out, [(c * t) % mod if mod else c * t for t in term], mod)
        return self.reduce(out, mod)

    def random_element(self, bound: int = 5, rng: Optional[random.Random] = None) -> Poly:
        r = rng or random
        return poly_trim([r.randint(-bound, bound) for _ in range(self.degree)])

# Experiment 1: the Frobenius congruence sigma(x) = x^p (mod p)

def frobenius_congruence_defect(ring: CyclotomicRing, x: Poly, p: int) -> Poly:
    """Return sigma_p(x) - x^p in Z[zeta_n]; Theorem A says p divides it."""
    return poly_sub(ring.power_map(x, p), ring.power(x, p))


def experiment_frobenius_congruence(trials: int = 4, seed: int = 20260804) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXPERIMENT 1 -- Frobenius congruence:  sigma_p(x) = x^p  (mod p)")
    print("=" * 78)
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    for n, p in [(5, 3), (7, 2), (8, 5), (12, 7)]:
        ring = CyclotomicRing(n)
        print(f"\n  n = {n:2d}   Phi_n = {poly_str(ring.phi)}   deg = {ring.degree}   p = {p}")
        for _ in range(trials):
            x = ring.random_element(4, rng)
            defect = frobenius_congruence_defect(ring, x, p)
            divisible = all(c % p == 0 for c in defect)
            quotient = [c // p for c in defect]
            status = "OK " if divisible else "FAIL"
            print(f"    [{status}] x = {poly_str(x):<28s} "
                  f"(sigma_p(x) - x^p)/p = {poly_str(quotient)}")
            assert divisible, "Theorem A violated"
    print("\n  All defects are divisible by p, as Theorem A predicts.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Experiment 2: Frobenius search at a prime Q above p, and uniqueness
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def irreducible_factor_mod_p(ring: CyclotomicRing, p: int) -> Poly:
    """A monic irreducible factor g of Phi_n mod p; Q = (p, g(zeta)) is a prime.

    The residue field Z[zeta]/Q is F_p[X]/(g), of size p^deg(g).  We take a
    factor of degree 1 whenever one exists (i.e. when p = 1 mod n), otherwise we
    split off a factor by trial division by all monic polynomials of small
    degree.  For the small parameters used in the demo this is ample.
    """
    f = [c % p for c in ring.phi]
    d = len(f) - 1
    for deg in range(1, d + 1):
        for coeffs in _monic_polys(deg, p):
            q, r = poly_divmod(f, coeffs, p)
            if not r:
                return coeffs
    raise RuntimeError("no factor found")


def _monic_polys(deg: int, p: int):
    """Enumerate monic polynomials of the given degree over F_p."""
    def rec(prefix: List[int], k: int):
        if k == 0:
            yield prefix + [1]
            return
        for c in range(p):
            yield from rec(prefix + [c], k - 1)
    return rec([], deg)


def is_arith_frobenius(ring: CyclotomicRing, m: int, p: int, g: Poly,
                       test_elements: Sequence[Poly]) -> bool:
    """Test sigma_m(x) = x^p mod Q for Q = (p, g(zeta)), on the given elements."""
    for x in test_elements:
        lhs = poly_mod(ring.power_map(x, m, p), g, p)
        rhs = poly_mod(ring.power(x, p, p), g, p)
        if poly_trim(lhs) != poly_trim(rhs):
            return False
    return True


def experiment_frobenius_search(seed: int = 7) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXPERIMENT 2 -- Frobenius search at Q | p:  exactly one power map wins")
    print("=" * 78)
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    for n, p in [(5, 3), (7, 3), (8, 5), (11, 2), (12, 7)]:
        ring = CyclotomicRing(n)
        g = irreducible_factor_mod_p(ring, p)
        tests = [ring.random_element(3, rng) for _ in range(6)] + [[0, 1], [1, 1]]
        winners = [m for m in range(1, n) if math.gcd(m, n) == 1
                   and is_arith_frobenius(ring, m, p, g, tests)]
        predicted = p % n
        print(f"\n  n = {n:2d}, p = {p}:  residue field F_{p}^{len(g) - 1} "
              f"via g = {poly_str(g, 'X')} mod {p}")
        print(f"    candidates m in (Z/{n})^*  : "
              f"{[m for m in range(1, n) if math.gcd(m, n) == 1]}")
        print(f"    Frobenius maps found       : {winners}")
        print(f"    predicted (m = p mod n)    : [{predicted}]")
        assert winners == [predicted], "Theorem C / rigidity violated"
    print("\n  In every case the Frobenius exists and is unique: it is sigma_p.")

def experiment_ramified_failure() -> None:

    print("=" * 78)

    print("  n of zeta is not invertible mod Q.  The hypothesis is necessary.")

# Experiment 4: class numbers and Hilbert class field degrees

def class_number_imaginary_quadratic(disc: int) -> int:
    """h(D) for a negative fundamental discriminant D, by counting reduced forms.

    A reduced positive definite form (a, b, c) with b^2 - 4ac = D satisfies
    |b| <= a <= c, and b >= 0 whenever |b| = a or a = c.
    """
    if disc >= 0 or disc % 4 not in (0, 1):
        raise ValueError("D must be a negative discriminant, D = 0 or 1 mod 4")
    count = 0
    a_max = int(math.isqrt(-disc // 3)) + 1
    for a in range(1, a_max + 1):
        for b in range(-a + 1, a + 1):
            num = b * b - disc
            if num % (4 * a):
                continue
            c = num // (4 * a)
            if c < a:
                continue
            if (a == c or abs(b) == a) and b < 0:
                continue
            count += 1
    return count


def fundamental_discriminant(d: int) -> int:
    """Discriminant of Q(sqrt(-d)) for squarefree d > 0."""
    return -d if (-d) % 4 == 1 else -4 * d


def squarefree(m: int) -> bool:
    k = 2
    while k * k <= m:
        if m % (k * k) == 0:
            return False
        k += 1
    return True


def experiment_class_numbers(limit: int = 60) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXPERIMENT 4 -- class numbers h_K and forced Hilbert class field degree")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  K = Q(sqrt(-d));  any Hilbert class field of K has degree exactly h_K,")
    print("  and equals K itself precisely when h_K = 1.\n")
    print(f"    {'d':>4s} {'disc':>6s} {'h_K':>5s}  {'[H:K] forced':>13s}  trivial?")
    trivial: List[int] = []
    by_class_number: Dict[int, List[int]] = {}
    for d in range(1, limit + 1):
        if not squarefree(d):
            continue
        D = fundamental_discriminant(d)
        h = class_number_imaginary_quadratic(D)
        by_class_number.setdefault(h, []).append(d)
        if h == 1:
            trivial.append(d)
        if d <= 30:
            print(f"    {d:4d} {D:6d} {h:5d}  {h:13d}  {'yes' if h == 1 else 'no'}")
    print(f"\n  Class number one for d <= {limit}: {trivial}")
    print("  (These are the Heegner values: 1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163.)")
    for h in sorted(by_class_number)[:6]:
        print(f"    h_K = {h}: d = {by_class_number[h][:10]}")
    assert trivial[:7] == [1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43]

# Experiment 5: the Minkowski discriminant bound
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def minkowski_discriminant_lower_bound(n: int, r2: int) -> float:
    """(pi/4)^(2 r2) * n^(2n) / (n!)^2 : a lower bound for |d_K| in degree n."""
    return (math.pi / 4.0) ** (2 * r2) * (n ** (2 * n)) / (math.factorial(n) ** 2)


def experiment_minkowski(max_degree: int = 8) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXPERIMENT 5 -- Minkowski bound forces |d_K| > 2 in degree >= 2")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  An everywhere-unramified number field has trivial different, hence")
    print("  |d_K| = 1.  The bound below shows that is impossible unless n = 1.\n")
    print(f"    {'n':>3s}  {'worst-case r2':>13s}  {'min |d_K| bound':>17s}  > 2 ?")
    for n in range(1, max_degree + 1):
        worst = max(range(0, n // 2 + 1),
                    key=lambda r2: -minkowski_discriminant_lower_bound(n, r2))
        bound = minkowski_discriminant_lower_bound(n, worst)
        flag = "yes" if bound > 2 else "no"
        print(f"    {n:3d}  {worst:13d}  {bound:17.4f}  {flag}")
        if n >= 2:
            assert bound > 2, "Minkowski bound unexpectedly weak"
    print("\n  Hence |d_K| = 1 forces [K:Q] = 1: Q has no unramified extension,")
    print("  so every Hilbert class field datum over Q is trivial, matching h_Q = 1.")

import math

Poly = List[int]


def _trim(a: Poly) -> Poly:
    b = list(a)
    while b and b[-1] == 0:
        b.pop()
    return b


def _divmod_int(a: Poly, m: Poly) -> Tuple[Poly, Poly]:
    q: Poly = [0] * max(0, len(a) - len(m) + 1)
    r = list(a)
    while _trim(r) and len(_trim(r)) >= len(m):
        r = _trim(r)
        s = len(r) - len(m)
        c = r[-1]
        q[s] = c
        for i, mi in enumerate(m):
            r[s + i] -= c * mi
    return _trim(q), _trim(r)


def cyclotomic(n: int) -> Poly:
    if n == 1:
        return [-1, 1]
    num: Poly = [0] * n + [1]
    num[0] = -1
    for d in range(1, n):
        if n % d == 0:
            num, rem = _divmod_int(num, cyclotomic(d))
            assert not rem
    return num


def poly_mul_modp(a: Poly, b: Poly, p: int) -> Poly:
    if not a or not b:
        return []
    out = [0] * (len(a) + len(b) - 1)
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai % p:
            for j, bj in enumerate(b):
                out[i + j] = (out[i + j] + ai * bj) % p
    return _trim(out)


def poly_divmod_modp(a: Poly, m: Poly, p: int) -> Tuple[Poly, Poly]:
    m = _trim([c % p for c in m])
    inv = pow(m[-1], -1, p)
    q: Poly = [0] * max(0, len(a) - len(m) + 1)
    r = [c % p for c in a]
    while _trim(r) and len(_trim(r)) >= len(m):
        r = _trim(r)
        s = len(r) - len(m)
        c = (r[-1] * inv) % p
        q[s] = c
        for i, mi in enumerate(m):
            r[s + i] = (r[s + i] - c * mi) % p
    return _trim(q), _trim(r)


def poly_gcd_modp(a: Poly, b: Poly, p: int) -> Poly:
    a, b = _trim([c % p for c in a]), _trim([c % p for c in b])
    while b:
        a, b = b, poly_divmod_modp(a, b, p)[1]
    if a:
        inv = pow(a[-1], -1, p)
        a = [(c * inv) % p for c in a]
    return a


def poly_powmod(a: Poly, e: int, m: Poly, p: int) -> Poly:
    result: Poly = [1]
    base = poly_divmod_modp(a, m, p)[1]
    while e:
        if e & 1:
            result = poly_divmod_modp(poly_mul_modp(result, base, p), m, p)[1]
        base = poly_divmod_modp(poly_mul_modp(base, base, p), m, p)[1]
        e >>= 1
    return result


def distinct_degree_profile(f: Poly, p: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Number of irreducible factors of each degree, for squarefree f mod p."""
    profile: Dict[int, int] = {}
    h = _trim([c % p for c in f])
    d = 0
    x_pow: Poly = [0, 1]
    while len(h) > 1:
        d += 1
        x_pow = poly_powmod(x_pow, p, h, p)
        g = poly_gcd_modp(_trim([(x_pow[i] if i < len(x_pow) else 0) - (1 if i == 1 else 0)
                                 for i in range(max(len(x_pow), 2))]), h, p)
        if len(g) > 1:
            profile[d] = (len(g) - 1) // d
            h = poly_divmod_modp(h, g, p)[0]
            x_pow = poly_divmod_modp(x_pow, h, p)[1] if len(h) > 1 else x_pow
    return profile


def multiplicative_order(p: int, n: int) -> int:
    assert math.gcd(p, n) == 1
    f, cur = 1, p % n
    while cur != 1 % n:
        cur = (cur * p) % n
        f += 1
    return f


def euler_phi(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for k in range(1, n + 1) if math.gcd(k, n) == 1)


def splitting_profile(n: int, p: int) -> Dict[str, int]:
    f = multiplicative_order(p, n)
    return {"residue_degree_f": f, "number_of_primes_g": euler_phi(n) // f,
            "degree_phi_n": euler_phi(n)}


def main() -> None:
    print("Splitting of p in Q(zeta_n), predicted by the Frobenius sigma_p alone")
    print("=" * 74)

          f"  {'factor degrees mod p':>24s}")
    for n in [5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16]:
        for p in [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13]:
            if n % p == 0:
                continue
            prof = splitting_profile(n, p)
            deg_profile = distinct_degree_profile(cyclotomic(n), p)
            observed = ", ".join(f"{cnt} of degree {deg}" for deg, cnt in sorted(deg_profile.items()))
            print(f"{n:>4d} {p:>4d} {prof['degree_phi_n']:>7d} {prof['residue_degree_f']:>13d}"
                  f" {prof['number_of_primes_g']:>10d}  {observed:>24s}")

    print("the residue degree f and hence the number g = phi(n)/f of primes above p.")

    print("Z[i] = Z[zeta_4] at Q = (1+i):  Phi_4 = X^2+1 = (X+1)^2 mod 2, so 2 RAMIFIES")

        print(f"  {name:<20s} (zeta -> zeta^{m}) is a Frobenius at Q: {ok}")
    print("Two distinct Frobenius maps: the hypothesis 'n invertible mod Q' is needed.")


def _frob_power_map(a: Poly, m: int, n: int, p: int) -> Poly:
    phi = cyclotomic(n)
    out: Poly = []
    for i, c in enumerate(a):
        if c % p:

            out = _trim([((out[k] if k < len(out) else 0) + c * (t[k] if k < len(t) else 0)) % p
                         for k in range(max(len(out), len(t)))])
    return poly_divmod_modp(out, [x % p for x in phi], p)[1]

Poly = List[int]


def _trim(a: Poly) -> Poly:
    b = list(a)

def poly_add(a: Poly, b: Poly) -> Poly:
    n = max(len(a), len(b))
    return _trim([(a[i] if i < len(a) else 0) + (b[i] if i < len(b) else 0) for i in range(n)])


def poly_sub(a: Poly, b: Poly) -> Poly:
    n = max(len(a), len(b))
    return _trim([(a[i] if i < len(a) else 0) - (b[i] if i < len(b) else 0) for i in range(n)])


def poly_mul(a: Poly, b: Poly) -> Poly:
    if not a or not b:
        return []
    out = [0] * (len(a) + len(b) - 1)
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        if ai:
            for j, bj in enumerate(b):
                out[i + j] += ai * bj
    return _trim(out)


def poly_divmod_monic(a: Poly, m: Poly) -> Tuple[Poly, Poly]:
    """Divide by a monic polynomial m over Z."""
    q: Poly = [0] * max(0, len(a) - len(m) + 1)
    r = list(a)

import math
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def minkowski_bound(n: int, r2: int) -> float:
    return (math.pi / 4.0) ** (2 * r2) * (n ** (2 * n)) / (math.factorial(n) ** 2)


def worst_case_bound(n: int) -> float:
    return min(minkowski_bound(n, r2) for r2 in range(0, n // 2 + 1))


def main() -> None:

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("minkowski_collapse.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote minkowski_collapse.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

// ---------- tiny BigInt polynomial arithmetic (little-endian coefficients) ----------

    q[s] = c; for (let i=0;i<m.length;i++) r[s+i] -= c*m[i];

  return [trim(q), trim(r)];

function cyclotomic(n) {

# Frobenius, Reciprocity, and the Shape of a Hilbert Class Field

*A guided tour: from a two-line congruence to the hardest open construction in
algebraic number theory.*

---

## 0. The question in one sentence

Number theory keeps discovering that **arithmetic** (which primes split, which stay
whole) and **symmetry** (the automorphisms of a field extension) are the same subject
in two costumes. The cleanest instance is the circle: adjoin a root of unity to the
rationals, and the symmetry group you get is a group of *residue classes*.

Fix an integer $n$ and let $\zeta$ be a primitive $n$-th root of unity, i.e. a number
with $\zeta^n = 1$ and no smaller positive power equal to $1$ — think of
$\zeta = e^{2\pi i/n}$. Every symmetry of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$ must send $\zeta$ to
another primitive root, so to $\zeta^m$ with $\gcd(m,n)=1$, and this gives an
isomorphism
$$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times \;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\; \mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)/\mathbb{Q}),
\qquad m \longmapsto \sigma_m : \zeta \mapsto \zeta^m .$$

The arithmetic side is the **Frobenius**. Fix a prime $p$ and a prime ideal $Q$ of the
ring $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]$ sitting above it, with residue cardinality $p$ over the
integers. A map $\sigma$ is an *arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$* if
$$\sigma(x) \equiv x^p \pmod{Q}\qquad\text{for every } x \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta].$$

The dictionary claims: **the Frobenius at $Q$ is the power map $\sigma_p$.** Let us see
it happen, then prove it, then find out how cheap the proof really is.

---

## 1. Play with it first

Turn the dials. Choose an order $n$ and a prime $p$: the widget draws how
$\sigma_p$ permutes the $n$-th roots of unity, checks the congruence
$\sigma_p(x) \equiv x^p \pmod p$ on a random element of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]$, and then
runs a brute-force search through *all* $\varphi(n)$ power maps looking for one that is
a Frobenius. Notice that the search never returns zero winners, and never returns two.

lengths are all equal to the multiplicative order $f$ of $p$ modulo $n$ — and that
number $f$ is exactly the *residue degree* of any prime of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]$ above
$p$, so the number of distinct primes above $p$ is $\varphi(n)/f$. The picture is
literally the factorisation of $p$, drawn on a circle. Golden dots are the fixed points.
</details>

## 2. The congruence that does all the work

Here is the first theorem, in full generality. No fields, no roots of unity, no
ramification.

> **Theorem (Frobenius congruence).** Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $p$ a prime, and
> $\zeta \in A$ any element. If $\sigma : A \to A$ is a ring homomorphism with
> $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^p$, then for every $x$ in the subring $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]$
> generated by $\zeta$,
> $$\sigma(x) \equiv x^{p} \pmod{pA}.$$

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal the proof (four lines, four ingredients)</strong></summary>

Let $T = \{x : \sigma(x) - x^p \in pA\}$. Since $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]$ is built from
integers and $\zeta$ using $+$ and $\times$, it suffices to check that $T$ contains both
and is closed under both.

- **Integers.** [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_little_theorem):
  $m^p \equiv m \pmod p$. And $\sigma$ fixes integers.
- **The generator.** $\sigma(\zeta) - \zeta^p = 0$ by hypothesis.
- **Products.** $\sigma(xy) - (xy)^p = (\sigma x - x^p)\sigma y + x^p(\sigma y - y^p)$.
- **Sums.** The [freshman's dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freshman%27s_dream):
  $p \mid \binom{p}{k}$ for $0<k<p$, so $(x+y)^p = x^p + y^p + p\,w$ with $w \in A$.

Add up, and you are done. Notice what never appeared: ramification indices,
decomposition groups, valuations, or even the assumption that $A$ is a domain.
</details>

The certificate is completely explicit: the difference $\sigma_p(x) - x^p$ is $p$ times
something, and that something can be written down.

{{algorithm:0}}

## 3. The converse: from congruence to *equality*

Guessing the converse is easy; the interesting question is what it costs.

> **Theorem (Frobenius determines the generator).** Let $S$ be an integral domain,
> $\zeta \in S$ with $\zeta^n = 1$, and let $Q$ be a prime of $S$ with residue
> cardinality $p$ over the base, and suppose $n \notin Q$. Then every arithmetic
> Frobenius $\sigma$ at $Q$ satisfies $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^p$ **exactly**, not merely
> modulo $Q$.

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal the proof (a small gem)</strong></summary>

Put $a = \sigma(\zeta)$, $b = \zeta^p$. Both are $n$-th roots of unity:
$a^n = \sigma(\zeta^n) = 1$ and $b^n = (\zeta^n)^p = 1$. And $a - b \in Q$, since
$\sigma$ is a Frobenius. Factor
$$0 = a^n - b^n = (a-b)\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a^i b^{\,n-1-i}.$$
Suppose $a \ne b$. In a domain the sum must vanish. But modulo $Q$ we have $a \equiv b$,
so every one of the $n$ terms is $\equiv b^{n-1}$, whence $n\,b^{n-1} \in Q$. Since
$b\cdot b^{n-1} = 1$, $b^{n-1}$ is a unit, so $n \in Q$ — contradiction. Hence $a=b$.
</details>

The moral: $n \notin Q$ says exactly that $X^n - 1$ stays
[separable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separable_polynomial) modulo $Q$, and
separability is what stops two distinct roots of unity from colliding.

Putting the two directions together:

> **Theorem (Characterisation and rigidity).** Let $S = \mathbb{Z}[\zeta]$ be a domain
> generated by a root of unity of order $n$, and $Q$ a prime with residue cardinality a
> prime $p$, with $p \in Q$ and $n \notin Q$. Then an endomorphism $\sigma$ over the
> base is an arithmetic Frobenius at $Q$ **iff** $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^p$. In
> particular the Frobenius at $Q$ is **unique** — with *no* unramifiedness hypothesis.

That last clause is stronger than the textbook statement, which needs $Q$ unramified.
Here uniqueness is free: the generator's image is forced, and a ring map is determined
by where it sends a generator.

$g = \varphi(n)/f$ of primes above $p$, hence the entire factorisation of $\Phi_n$ modulo
$p$. The script cross-checks the prediction against a real polynomial factorisation, and
then exhibits the one place rigidity fails: the ramified prime $(1+i)$ of the Gaussian
integers, where $4 \in Q$ and *both* the identity and complex conjugation are Frobenius

## 5. The other half: what a Hilbert class field must be

Now the hard direction of the dictionary. For a number field $K$, the
[ideal class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_class_group)
$\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal{O}_K)$ measures the failure of unique factorisation in the ring of
integers $\mathcal{O}_K$; its size is the class number $h_K$. The **Hilbert class field**
is supposed to be a finite Galois extension $H/K$, unramified at every prime, with
$$\mathrm{Gal}(H/K) \;\simeq\; \mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal{O}_K).$$

Bundle that wish list into a single object — a *Hilbert class field datum* — and ask what
it forces, before knowing whether it exists:

- **Degree.** $[H:K] = h_K$, because a finite Galois extension has as many automorphisms
  as its degree.
- **Abelianness.** $\mathrm{Gal}(H/K)$ is abelian, because it is isomorphic to a class group.
- **Triviality detector.** $H = K$ **iff** $h_K = 1$.
- **Well-posedness.** Any two such data over the same $K$ have the same degree.
- **Realisation.** If $\mathcal{O}_K$ is a principal ideal ring, $H = K$ works.

Each is a one-line consequence — and together they are a falsifiability harness: a
proposed construction of the wrong degree, or with a nonabelian group, is wrong on the
spot. Compute the target for yourself:

{{algorithm:2}}

{{visualization:1}}

<details>
<summary><strong>Why counting reduced forms computes the class number</strong></summary>

For an imaginary quadratic field of discriminant $D<0$, ideal classes correspond
bijectively to classes of positive definite
[binary quadratic forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_quadratic_form)
$ax^2+bxy+cy^2$ of discriminant $b^2-4ac = D$, and each class has a unique *reduced*
representative: $|b| \le a \le c$, with $b \ge 0$ when $|b| = a$ or $a = c$. So counting
reduced triples counts ideal classes. The orange bars in the chart are the nine
[Heegner numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heegner_number)
$1,2,3,7,11,19,43,67,163$ — the imaginary quadratic fields with unique factorisation,
and exactly the ones that are their own Hilbert class field.
</details>

## 6. The first real test: $\mathbb{Q}$ has nowhere to go

$h_\mathbb{Q} = 1$, so the prediction is that the only Hilbert class field datum over
$\mathbb{Q}$ is the trivial one. Proving that is *not* bookkeeping — it needs a genuine
nineteenth-century theorem.

> **Theorem.** If $K$ is a number field in which every prime of $\mathcal{O}_K$ is
> unramified over $\mathbb{Z}$, then $K = \mathbb{Q}$.

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal the three-step collapse</strong></summary>

1. A prime divides the [different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal)
   exactly when it ramifies. If nothing ramifies, the different is the unit ideal.
2. The absolute norm of the different is $|d_K|$, so $|d_K| = 1$.
3. [Minkowski's bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski%27s_bound), from the
   geometry of numbers, gives $|d_K| > 2$ for every field of degree $\ge 2$.

Steps 2 and 3 collide, so the degree is $1$.
</details>

{{visualization:2}}

The shaded region in that plot is the empty space between what unramifiedness demands
($|d_K| = 1$) and what geometry permits. Two completely independent derivations — one
from the reciprocity isomorphism, one from lattice packing — agree that
$\mathbb{Q}$ is its own Hilbert class field. That agreement is the point: it is a real
consistency check on the definitions, not a tautology.
